title: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
topicTitle: Bandwidth and propagation of electromagnetic waves
notes: Bandwidth is the range of frequencies a signal or a channel occupies. A wider message, such as television, needs a wider channel than speech. Two stations must be separated by at least their bandwidths or they overlap.

A ground wave travels along the surface of the Earth. The ground absorbs more energy at higher frequency, so ground-wave broadcast is used for the lower radio frequencies and does not reach around the world.

A sky wave is sent upward and can be returned by the ionosphere. That is how short-wave radio crosses long distances. The ionosphere is not a metal mirror at every frequency: above a critical frequency the wave passes through.
A space wave travels in a straight line from a high transmitting antenna to the receiver. Television and FM use it. The Earth's curve limits the range to a little beyond the geometric horizon.
For an antenna at height h above a spherical Earth of radius R, the horizon distance is about √(2 R h) when h is much smaller than R. A higher mast sees farther.
The same information can be sent in a narrow band by slowing it down, or in a wide band by sending it quickly. The channel must be at least as wide as the signal.

keyPoints: Bandwidth is the spread of frequencies used.
Sky waves reflect from the ionosphere.
Space waves travel in line of sight.
summary: Bandwidth is the frequency width a signal needs. Ground waves follow the Earth at lower frequencies, sky waves can bounce from the ionosphere, and space waves travel in line of sight. The radio horizon of a mast of height h is about the square root of 2 R h.
